# Appendix: Proofs {#sec-appendix}

## Proof of Proposition [-@prp-moments]

For the binary distribution, the moments follow directly from the definition:

$$
\kappa^B=\frac{1}{2u_\ell}+\frac{1}{2u_H},
\qquad
\nu^B=\frac{u_\ell+u_H}{2}.
$$

For the uniform distribution, let the density be

$$
f(v)=\frac{1}{2\delta}\mathbf{1}_{[\mu-\delta,\mu+\delta]}(v).
$$

Because $[\mu-\delta,\mu+\delta]\subset(0,\infty)$ is compact and $v\mapsto v^{-1/2}$ is continuous on it, $v^{-1/2}$ is Lebesgue integrable. Let $u=\sqrt v$; this is a $C^1$ diffeomorphism, with $dv=2u\,du$. Hence

$$
\kappa^U
=\frac{1}{2\delta}\int_{\mu-\delta}^{\mu+\delta}v^{-1/2}\,dv
=\frac{1}{2\delta}\cdot\bigl[2\sqrt v\bigr]_{\mu-\delta}^{\mu+\delta}
=\frac{u_H-u_\ell}{\delta}.
$$

Similarly, $v\mapsto v^{1/2}$ is also Lebesgue integrable, so

$$
\nu^U
=\frac{1}{2\delta}\int_{\mu-\delta}^{\mu+\delta}v^{1/2}\,dv
=\frac{1}{2\delta}\cdot\left[\frac{2}{3}v^{3/2}\right]_{\mu-\delta}^{\mu+\delta}
=\frac{u_H^3-u_\ell^3}{3\delta}.
$$

To compare $\kappa^B$ and $\kappa^U$, note first that $v\mapsto v^{-1/2}$ is strictly convex on $(0,\infty)$. Jensen's inequality therefore implies

$$
\kappa^B=\E_{\mathrm{binary}}[V_L^{-1/2}]
>
\left(\E_{\mathrm{binary}}[V_L]\right)^{-1/2}
=\mu^{-1/2}.
$$

Moreover, since $u_H^2-u_\ell^2=2\delta$,

$$
\kappa^U=\frac{u_H-u_\ell}{\delta}=\frac{2}{u_H+u_\ell},
\qquad
\kappa^B=\frac{1}{2u_\ell}+\frac{1}{2u_H}
=\frac{u_H+u_\ell}{2u_\ell u_H}.
$$

Hence

$$
\kappa^B-\kappa^U
=\frac{(u_H+u_\ell)^2-4u_\ell u_H}{2u_\ell u_H(u_H+u_\ell)}
=\frac{(u_H-u_\ell)^2}{2u_\ell u_H(u_H+u_\ell)}
>0.
$$

Therefore $\kappa^B>\kappa^U$.

## Proof of Proposition [-@prp-ss]

From @eq-brl, labor's best response for type $v$ is $x_L^*(x_M;v)=\sqrt{vx_M}-x_M$. Substituting into @eq-um gives

$$
U_M(x_L^*,x_M;V)
=\frac{x_M}{x_M+\sqrt{vx_M}-x_M}V-x_M
=V\sqrt{\frac{x_M}{v}}-x_M.
$$

Taking expectation over $v$,

$$
\E[U_M]=V\sqrt{x_M}\,\E[v^{-1/2}]-x_M
=V\sqrt{x_M}\,\kappa-x_M.
$$

The first- and second-order conditions are

$$
\frac{\partial \E[U_M]}{\partial x_M}
=\frac{V\kappa}{2\sqrt{x_M}}-1=0,
\qquad
\frac{\partial^2 \E[U_M]}{\partial x_M^2}
=-\frac{V\kappa}{4x_M^{3/2}}<0,
$$

so the unique maximizer is $x_M^{\mathrm{SS}}=V^2\kappa^2/4$. Then @eq-brl implies

$$
x_L^{\mathrm{SS}}(v)
=\sqrt{v\cdot\frac{V^2\kappa^2}{4}}-\frac{V^2\kappa^2}{4}
=\frac{V\kappa}{2}\sqrt v-\frac{V^2\kappa^2}{4}.
$$

Substituting into @eq-ul and @eq-um yields

$$
U_L^{\mathrm{SS}}(v)
=\frac{x_L^{\mathrm{SS}}}{x_L^{\mathrm{SS}}+x_M^{\mathrm{SS}}}v-x_L^{\mathrm{SS}}
=\left(\sqrt v-\frac{V\kappa}{2}\right)^2,
$$

$$
U_M^{\mathrm{SS}}(v)
=\frac{x_M^{\mathrm{SS}}}{x_L^{\mathrm{SS}}+x_M^{\mathrm{SS}}}V-x_M^{\mathrm{SS}}
=\frac{V^2\kappa}{2\sqrt v}-\frac{V^2\kappa^2}{4}.
$$

Finally,

$$
\E[U_L^{\mathrm{SS}}]
=\E\!\left[v-V\kappa\sqrt v+\frac{V^2\kappa^2}{4}\right]
=\mu-V\kappa\nu+\frac{V^2\kappa^2}{4},
$$

$$
\E[U_M^{\mathrm{SS}}]
=\E\!\left[\frac{V^2\kappa}{2\sqrt v}-\frac{V^2\kappa^2}{4}\right]
=\frac{V^2\kappa}{2}\E[v^{-1/2}]-\frac{V^2\kappa^2}{4}
=\frac{V^2\kappa^2}{4}.
$$

## Proof of Proposition [-@prp-ml]

In ML, stage 2 still gives labor's type-contingent best response $x_L^*(x_M;v)=\sqrt{vx_M}-x_M$. Therefore management solves

$$
\max_{x_M\ge 0}\;\E\!\left[V\sqrt{\frac{x_M}{V_L}}-x_M\right]
=\max_{x_M\ge 0}\;\left(V\sqrt{x_M}\,\kappa-x_M\right),
$$

which is exactly the SS problem. The same first- and second-order conditions imply the same optimal $x_M$, and @eq-brl then yields the same $x_L(v)$. Hence all payoffs coincide with SS.

## Proof of Proposition [-@prp-separating]

Labor solves

$$
\max_{x_L\ge 0}\;W(x_L;v)=\max_{x_L\ge 0}\left(\frac{v}{\sqrt V}\sqrt{x_L}-x_L\right).
$$

The first-order condition is

$$
\frac{v}{2\sqrt{Vx_L}} - 1 = 0
\quad\Rightarrow\quad
x_L^{\mathrm{LM}}(v)=\frac{v^2}{4V}.
$$

The second-order condition is

$$
\frac{\partial^2 W}{\partial x_L^2}=-\frac{v}{4\sqrt V}x_L^{-3/2}<0,
$$

so this is the unique global optimum. Then @eq-brm implies

$$
x_M^{\mathrm{LM}}(v)
=\sqrt{V\cdot\frac{v^2}{4V}}-\frac{v^2}{4V}
=\frac{v(2V-v)}{4V}.
$$

Substituting into @eq-ul and @eq-um yields @eq-ul-lm and @eq-um-lm.

## Proof of Proposition [-@prp-no-pool]

The proof has two steps.

First, show that equilibrium effort is one-to-one in type. Define

$$
\phi:[\mu-\delta,\mu+\delta]\to\mathbb{R},
\qquad
\phi(v)=\frac{v^2}{4V}.
$$

Because $\mu>\delta>0$, the support $[\mu-\delta,\mu+\delta]$ lies in $(0,\infty)$. Hence, for every $v$ in the support,

$$
\phi'(v)=\frac{v}{2V}>0.
$$

Therefore $\phi$ is strictly increasing on the support and thus injective. Equivalently, if $v\neq v'$, then

$$
\phi(v)\neq \phi(v').
$$

So distinct types cannot share the same optimal effort. Any candidate strategy that assigns the same effort to two different types is incompatible with the injectivity of $\phi$.

Second, prove strict global incentive compatibility of truthful play. Fix any true type $v$ and any $s\neq v$. If type $v$ chooses the effort associated with type $s$,

$$
x_L=\frac{s^2}{4V},
$$

then, after management responds according to @eq-brm, type $v$ obtains

$$
\tilde{U}(v,s)
=\frac{v}{\sqrt{V}}\cdot\frac{s}{2\sqrt{V}}-\frac{s^2}{4V}
=\frac{2vs-s^2}{4V}.
$$

Truthful play yields

$$
U(v,v)=\frac{v^2}{4V}.
$$

The payoff difference is

$$
U(v,v)-\tilde{U}(v,s)
=\frac{v^2-2vs+s^2}{4V}
=\frac{(v-s)^2}{4V}>0
\qquad\forall s\neq v.
$$

This difference is a positive-definite quadratic form and is strictly positive for every $s\neq v$. Hence any strategy that asks type $v$ to choose $s^2/(4V)$ with $s\neq v$ is strictly dominated by truthful play.

In the binary-type special case, this condition corresponds exactly to the main-text constraints `IC_H` and `IC_L`. Those two constraints jointly are necessary and sufficient for the separating candidate to be feasible. Necessity follows because a separating equilibrium must rule out imitation in both directions. Sufficiency follows because, given the continuation best response in @eq-brm, once both IC constraints hold, each type optimally chooses its own action.

Let

$$
D(v,s)\equiv U(v,v)-\tilde U(v,s)=\frac{(v-s)^2}{4V}.
$$

For fixed $s$, $D(v,s)$ is zero only at $v=s$, and

$$
\frac{\partial D(v,s)}{\partial v}=\frac{v-s}{2V}
$$

changes sign at that point. This gives the single-crossing representation. But no separate single-crossing argument is needed here, because $D(v,s)>0$ for every $s\neq v$ already delivers the stronger global strict IC result.

Because management's continuation best response depends only on observed effort and the parameter $V$, not on posterior beliefs, beliefs cannot overturn this deviation argument. Therefore no pooling or semi-separating behavior can arise in PBE, and there is no parameter region in which pooling is feasible. The LM subgame admits a unique PBE, and it is separating.

## Proof of the LM Expected-Payoff Formulas

From @eq-ul-lm, $U_L^{\mathrm{LM}}(v)=v^2/(4V)$, so

$$
\E[U_L^{\mathrm{LM}}]
=\E\!\left[\frac{V_L^2}{4V}\right]
=\frac{\E[V_L^2]}{4V}
=\frac{\mu^2+\sigma^2}{4V}.
$$

From @eq-um-lm,

$$
\E[U_M^{\mathrm{LM}}]
=\E\!\left[\frac{(2V-V_L)^2}{4V}\right]
=\frac{4V^2-4V\E[V_L]+\E[V_L^2]}{4V}
=\frac{4V^2-4V\mu+\mu^2+\sigma^2}{4V}.
$$

## Proof of Proposition [-@prp-stage1-br]

From the stage-1 payoff matrix:

- if management chooses S, labor compares $\E[U_L^{\mathrm{LM}}]$ from F with $\E[U_L^{\mathrm{SS}}]$ from S, so the difference is $\Delta_L$;
- if management chooses F, labor compares SS with ML, which are equal;
- if labor chooses F, management compares SS with LM, so the difference is $\Delta_M$;
- if labor chooses S, management compares ML with SS, which are equal.

The stated best-response correspondences follow immediately.

## Proof of Proposition [-@prp-stage1-ne]

Inspect each cell of the stage-1 payoff matrix:

- at $(S,F)$, labor compares ML with SS and management compares ML with SS; both are weakly indifferent, so $(S,F)$ is a Nash equilibrium;
- at $(F,F)$, labor is indifferent, while management prefers F to S if and only if $\E[U_M^{\mathrm{SS}}]\ge \E[U_M^{\mathrm{LM}}]$, that is, $\Delta_M\ge 0$;
- at $(S,S)$, management is indifferent, while labor prefers S to F if and only if $\E[U_L^{\mathrm{SS}}]\ge \E[U_L^{\mathrm{LM}}]$, that is, $\Delta_L\le 0$;
- at $(F,S)$, labor prefers F to S if and only if $\Delta_L\ge 0$, while management prefers S to F if and only if $\E[U_M^{\mathrm{LM}}]\ge \E[U_M^{\mathrm{SS}}]$, that is, $\Delta_M\le 0$.

This proves the proposition.

## Proof of Theorem [-@thm-timing-eq]

For a strategy profile $(a_L,a_M)\in\{F,S\}^2$, $(a_L,a_M)$ is a Nash equilibrium if and only if no player can gain strictly from a unilateral deviation.

First consider $(S,F)$. If Labor deviates from $S$ to $F$, the outcome changes from $(S,F)$ to $(F,F)$, that is, from ML to SS. Labor's payoff changes from $\E[U_L^{\mathrm{ML}}]$ to $\E[U_L^{\mathrm{SS}}]$. By @eq-eul-ml, these two payoffs are equal, so Labor has no strict deviation incentive. If Management deviates from $F$ to $S$, the outcome changes from $(S,F)$ to $(S,S)$, again from ML to SS. Management's payoff changes from $\E[U_M^{\mathrm{ML}}]$ to $\E[U_M^{\mathrm{SS}}]$. By @eq-eum-ml, these two payoffs are also equal, so Management has no strict deviation incentive. Hence $(S,F)$ is a Nash equilibrium for every parameter value.

Now consider $(F,S)$. If Labor deviates from $F$ to $S$, its payoff changes from $\E[U_L^{\mathrm{LM}}]$ to $\E[U_L^{\mathrm{SS}}]$. Labor does not deviate if and only if

$$
\E[U_L^{\mathrm{LM}}]\ge \E[U_L^{\mathrm{SS}}],
$$

that is,

$$
\Delta_L\ge 0.
$$

If Management deviates from $S$ to $F$, the profile changes from $(F,S)$ to $(F,F)$, that is, to SS. Management's payoff changes from $\E[U_M^{\mathrm{LM}}]$ to $\E[U_M^{\mathrm{SS}}]=\E[U_M^{\mathrm{ML}}]$. Management does not deviate if and only if

$$
\E[U_M^{\mathrm{LM}}]\ge \E[U_M^{\mathrm{ML}}],
$$

that is,

$$
\Delta_M\le 0.
$$

Both conditions must hold simultaneously. Therefore $(F,S)$ is a Nash equilibrium if and only if $\Delta_L\ge 0$ and $\Delta_M\le 0$. Substituting @eq-eul-ss, @eq-eum-ml, @eq-eul-lm, and @eq-eum-lm then yields the explicit inequalities in the theorem.

## Proof of Proposition [-@prp-ex-ante-decomp]

Starting from $R(v)\equiv U_L^{\mathrm{SS}}(v)-U_L^{\mathrm{LM}}(v)$ and taking expectation over $V_L$,

$$
\E[R(V_L)]
=
\E[U_L^{\mathrm{SS}}]-\E[U_L^{\mathrm{LM}}]
=
-\Delta_L.
$$

This proves the proposition.

## Proof of Proposition [-@prp-exact-condition]

Type $v$ ex post prefers to move first if and only if

$$
R(v)\le 0.
$$

By definition,

$$
R(v)\leq 0
\iff
\left(\sqrt{v}-\frac{V\kappa}{2}\right)^2\leq\frac{v^2}{4V}.
$$

Because $v>0$, the square root of the right-hand side, $\frac{v}{2\sqrt V}$, is strictly positive. Hence the preceding inequality is equivalent to

$$
\left|\sqrt{v}-\frac{V\kappa}{2}\right|
\leq
\frac{v}{2\sqrt{V}}.
$$

Expanding the absolute-value inequality gives the double inequality

$$
\sqrt{v}-\frac{v}{2\sqrt{V}}
\leq
\frac{V\kappa}{2}
\leq
\sqrt{v}+\frac{v}{2\sqrt{V}}.
$$

This proves the proposition.

## Proof of Proposition [-@prp-mgmt]

From @eq-eum-ml and @eq-eum-lm,

$$
\E\!\left[U_M^{\mathrm{ML}}\right]=\frac{V^2\kappa^2}{4},
\qquad
\E\!\left[U_M^{\mathrm{LM}}\right]=\frac{4V^2-4V\mu+\mu^2+\sigma^2}{4V}.
$$

Therefore the condition $\E[U_M^{\mathrm{ML}}]\ge\E[U_M^{\mathrm{LM}}]$ is exactly @eq-mgmt-cond. Note that Theorem [-@thm-timing-eq] requires $\Delta_M \le 0$ for LM to be an equilibrium, so the inequality is reversed there.

## Proof of the Welfare Formulas in Section @sec-welfare

By definition, $W=U_L+U_M$. For SS, and for ML because it is payoff-equivalent,

$$
\E[W^{\mathrm{SS}}]
=\E[U_L^{\mathrm{SS}}]+\E[U_M^{\mathrm{SS}}]
=\left(\mu-V\kappa\nu+\frac{V^2\kappa^2}{4}\right)+\frac{V^2\kappa^2}{4}
=\mu-V\kappa\nu+\frac{V^2\kappa^2}{2}.
$$

For LM,

$$
\E[W^{\mathrm{LM}}]
=\E[U_L^{\mathrm{LM}}]+\E[U_M^{\mathrm{LM}}]
=\frac{\mu^2+\sigma^2}{4V}+\frac{4V^2-4V\mu+\mu^2+\sigma^2}{4V}
=V-\mu+\frac{\mu^2+\sigma^2}{2V}.
$$
